title: M92, NGC 6341
caption: The globular cluster M92, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This approximately true-color picture shows M92, also cataloged as NGC 6341, a globular cluster in the constellation Hercules. Under excellent sky conditions it can even be seen with the naked eye.

A globular cluster is a tightly packed, roughly spherical collection of very old stars bound together by gravity. M92 lies about 28000 light-years away and measures more than 100 light-years across, which means an enormous number of stars are squeezed into the ball.

M92 has a well-known neighbor on the sky, the globular cluster M13, also in Hercules. Compared with M13, M92 is slightly farther away and a little younger. Clusters like these are valuable to astronomers because all their stars formed at about the same time, making them natural laboratories for studying how stars age.
scale: M92 is about 28000 light-years away and more than 100 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak recorded M92 in visible light through B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-color picture.
understand.eye: To the naked eye M92 is at best a faint smudge. The telescope's exposures resolve it into many individual stars.

explore: The images for this picture were taken in June 1996 using B, V and R filters with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, part of its Warner and Swasey Observatory, near Tucson, Arizona, on Kitt Peak, as part of the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The field is 28.8 arcminutes across.
alt: A dense, round ball of stars set in a field of scattered stars.
